Guernsey Economic Activity Slows Sharply Amid Norovirus Outbreak and Renewed Lockdown Measures

Businesses across Guernsey are reporting sharp declines in trade as the island grapples with a widespread norovirus outbreak and the government’s imposition of renewed lockdown measures. The restrictions, which came into effect last week, include the closure of non-essential retail, hospitality venues, and most public-facing services in an effort to curb surging case numbers.

According to figures released by the Guernsey Chamber of Commerce, overall economic activity has dropped by an estimated 35% in the past week. Retail footfall in St Peter Port is down by 80%, while hospitality bookings have “evaporated overnight,” said Kate Le Page, spokesperson for the Guernsey Hospitality Association. “We support the government’s health measures, but the impact on our sector is immediate and severe,” she added.

The States of Guernsey has ordered schools, leisure centres, and gyms to close, with only essential retailers—such as supermarkets and pharmacies—permitted to operate under strict capacity limits. All gatherings, indoors and outdoors, are currently prohibited. “We understand the hardship these measures cause, but our priority is to protect public health and maintain essential services,” stated Dr. Andrew Carre, Guernsey’s Director of Public Health.

Logistics and supply chains have also been disrupted, with ferry operator Channelisles Shipping Services announcing reduced freight schedules due to staff shortages and increased sanitation protocols. “We are doing everything possible to keep goods moving, but delays are likely,” confirmed managing director Ben Torode.

Trade unions are urging the States to expand emergency support for workers and small businesses. “Many employees are worried about their jobs,” said Joelle Girard, chair of the Guernsey Workers’ Union. “We need urgent financial assistance to prevent lasting damage.”

With no clear end date for the restrictions, local business groups are calling for a roadmap to reopening. “Certainty is critical,” said Chamber president Michael de la Mare. “We need to plan ahead to ensure Guernsey’s economic resilience.”
